en: Advayavajra’s Works 8. *Caturmudrā[niścaya/ānvaya]*;
most likely *Caturmudrānvaya*, cf. note to the colophon.
Edited by MM Hara Prasad Shastri in *Advayavajrasaṃgraha*, GOS 1927, Baroda;
edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kenkyūkai, Vol. 2.
In *Taishō Daigaku Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Nenpō* (Annual of the Institute for Comprehensive Studies of Buddhism, Taishō University), No. 11, 1989, pp. (92/253)–(106/239).
Oṃ. Homage to the glorious Vajrasattva.
Thus—
Having first prostrated to Vajrasattva, who is identical with pure gnosis,
this sequence of mudrās is set forth in brief for the sake of one's own awakening.

For here, those of deluded minds, wandering through confusion regarding the lineage of the mudrās, roam the ocean of existence in suffering. To enable them to easily realize the meaning of the four mudrās, the sādhana of great bliss is established in accordance with the tantras.

The four mudrās are the action-mudrā (karmamudrā), the dharma-mudrā, the great-mudrā (mahāmudrā), and the commitment-mudrā (samayamudrā). Among these, the nature of the action-mudrā is now described. Action refers to the mental activity of body, speech, and mind; the mudrā that is dominated by this is of the nature of conceptual construction. Within that action-mudrā, joys arise, differentiated according to the distinctions of the moments (kṣaṇa).
From the knowledge of the moment comes the knowledge of bliss, which is established in the syllable E-VAM.
% HeTa II.iii.5cd. % Also quoted in Rāmapāla’s Sekanirdeśapañjikā, folio 3 verso (94/251).

There are four joys: joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), innate joy (*sahajānanda*), and the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*). Otherwise: having observed the object between the supreme and the cessation, make it firm.
This which has been stated is also cited in Kumāracandra’s *Ratnāvalī* (p.
102), yet it is not consistent.

There are four moments: *vicitra*, *vipāka*, *vilakṣaṇa*, and *vimarda*. One should understand that the *vilakṣaṇa* is placed in the middle during the consecration (*seka*). Furthermore, in *haṭhayoga*, one should understand that the *sahaja* and *vilakṣaṇa* are situated at the end.
Regarding this, it was taught by the Blessed One in the context of Haṭhayoga:

"All that is innate (*sahaja*) is designated as 'innate' because it conforms to the shadow of the innate. The shadow of the innate brings about a gnosis (*jñāna*) similar to the innate. Thus, the innate is the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*). For this very reason, there is no arising of the innate within the gnosis of wisdom; for the so-called "innate" is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of all phenomena, characterized by being unconditioned (*akṛtrima*). Therefore, having obtained the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) arises.

Outflow (*nisyanda*) is a similar flow. Similarity is, for example, like the reflection of a face placed in a mirror; it is not the face itself, neither something previously established nor something newly produced.
Siddham. Although that very reflection on the face produces only a semblance, people nevertheless become satisfied through delusion, thinking, "I have seen my own face.

In the same way, teachers of poor intellect, having attained the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), produce satisfaction, thinking, "The innate (*sahaja*) has been experienced. And being thus satisfied, they do not even know the report of the Seal of Dharma (*dharmamudrā*). For those who do not know the Seal of Dharma, how can the unartificial state called the Innate arise through the mere artificial Seal of Action (*karmamudrā*)?

From a cause of its own kind, only an effect of its own kind arises, and not from a cause of a different kind. Just as a rice sprout arises from a rice seed, and not from *kodrava* grain, so too, from the presence of the uncontrived *dharmamudrā*, the uncontrived *sahaja* arises. Therefore, the *dharmamudrā* alone is the cause; through the metaphorical attribution of difference (*bhedopacāra*) to what is non-different, it is [designated] as the *mahāmudrā*.
Why, then, was it said by the Blessed One?
That divine [mandala] in the shape of the letter *E*, adorned in its center with the syllable *Vaṃ*,
is the abode of all happiness and a jewel-casket for the Buddhas.
% HeTa II.iii.4. % Also quoted in Vajrapāṇi’s *Laghutantraṭīkā*, p. 48. % Also quoted in Rāmapāla’s *Sekanirdeśapañjikā*, folio 3 recto.
Thus:

because it resembles the shadow of the Buddha, the *karaṇḍaka* is the place, the support. Therefore, for the woman who is the limb of action (*karmāṅganā*), the lotus is a mine of jewels consisting of a mass of bliss.

When, through the union of the juices of the churning stick, the churner, the *bola*, and the *kakkola*, the conventional bodhicitta enters within the jewel of the *avadhūtī*, then a gnosis arises called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) and also known as "other innate" (*aparasahaja*). That is not the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the [true] innate.

In its own nature, it is endowed with the four moments of the triad of wisdom (*prajñā*), gnosis (*jñāna*), and bliss (*ānanda*); this is said to be the natural outflow (*niṣyandaphala*) of the *karmamudrā* in the context of initiation and *haṭhayoga*.
This concludes the first section: "The Instruction on the Natural Outflow of the *Karmamudrā*."

OṂ—The Dharma-mudrā. She whose nature is the Dharmadhātu, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), uncontrived, devoid of arising, having compassion as her essence, uniquely beautiful through supreme bliss, serving as the means (*upāya*), and whose innate nature (*sahajasvabhāva*) is eternal by way of continuous flow—she who...
[is this].
That which is inseparable due to the coemergent arising (*sahajodaya*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) is designated as the *dharmamudrā*.

Its other characteristic should be understood from the instruction of the Guru as being like the rays of the sun within the darkness of confused ignorance, and as being free from the thorns of delusion even as small as a blade of grass or a husk. It should be understood as the single nature of the three worlds, thoroughly integrated with all earth, water, wind, and fire; and it should be understood as the indivisibility of waveless emptiness and compassion. And it was said by the Blessed One:
"The *lalanā* exists by the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), and the *rasanā* is established as method (*upāya*)."
The Avadhūtī, however, is in the middle region, free from the grasped and the grasper.
Also in the *Jñānodayatantra* (p.

10): "The path should be known by one who is skillful even through the aspect of suchness (*tathatā*), by way of its proximate aspect. Through the diligent and uninterrupted cultivation of the path within the knowledge of the path, there arises the direct realization of cessation, which is the innate nature (*sahajasvabhāva*)."
And so it has been said:
"Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added."
Reality must be seen as it truly is; one who sees reality is liberated.
Āryadeva’s *Caryāmelāpakapradīpa*, p.
102; also quoted in Mahāsukhavajra’s commentary on the *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa* (f. 11b6).

And in the anonymous commentary on the *Sampuṭodbhavatantra* (MS Kaiser Library 228 [NGMPP C 26/1], f. 3v6–7). A verse with a similar first half is quoted from the *Kālacakra-mūlatantra* in the *Vimalaprabhā* ad KCT 5.127 (VP vol. 3, p. 91). [This is Haru’s note from the CMTcomm. input; I have not personally seen the manuscript.]

Lalanā and rasanā—avadhūtī resides in the space between them. For one whose mental state has attained the single nature of the co-emergent (*sahaja*) of all phenomena through the instruction of a true guru, that very [avadhūtī] becomes the cause for mahāmudrā by way of its non-difference from the dharma-mudrā.
This concludes the second section: the exposition of the fruition as the maturation of the dharma-mudrā.

ĀḤ Mahāmudrā! It is called *mahāmudrā* because it is both great (*mahatī*) and a seal (*mudrā*). Mahāmudrā should be known as being without intrinsic nature, free from the obscurations of the knowable and so forth, resembling the cloudless autumn sky at midday, the support for all prosperity, whose single nature is both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa, whose body is non-referential compassion, and whose sole form is great bliss. And thus: "Phenomena that are not brought to mind are wholesome; phenomena that are brought to mind are unwholesome."
And in the teaching [of the] *Āryasarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṅkāramahāyānasūtra*, p. 109:
"One whose intention is non-conceptual, whose mind is non-abiding..."
Homage be to you, who are without mindfulness or mental attention, and free from any object of focus.
% \M id. *Pañcatathāgatamudrāvivaraṇa* p. 52. % *Amanasikārādhāra* pp. 136–137.
Thus, that which is designated as "Mahāmudrā" produces the fruit known as Samayamudrā by means of that Mahāmudrā, whose nature is inconceivable.
This is the third [section], the instruction on the fruit of the purity of Mahāmudrā.

HŪṂ, the pledge-mudrā (*samayamudrā*). That which is the radiance of Vajradhara in the form of Heruka for the sake of sentient beings—by way of the nature of the forms of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, and by way of a translucent form—is designated as the pledge-mudrā.

Having taken up that *samayamudrā*, the masters visualize the wheel of the *samayamudrā* by conceptualizing the fivefold gnosis as fivefold—namely, through the mirror-like, the equality, the discerning, the performance-of-duty, and the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* [gnoses]. By means of the *ādiyoga*, the *maṇḍalarājāgrī*, the *karmarājāgrī*, the *binduyoga*, and the *sūkṣmayoga*, they meditate upon the wheel of the *samayamudrā*. Through this, they become those who have performed merit; consequently, they do not become distinct from the fruit of the *dharmamudrā*.
Because the cause is restricted to its specific object, only a corresponding effect arises.

Because of the statement, "It is untraced," therefore, through the piercing of the innate accomplishment (*sahajasiddhi*), those entities such as the stable and the moving, which are imagined by the ignorant, become the cause of perfect awakening. By this, the *Trailokyacakra* is well-spoken.
And so it was said by the Blessed One:
"There is no recitation of mantras, no austerity, and no fire-offering."
There is neither the mandala-member nor the mandala;
that is the recitation of mantra, that is austerity, that is the fire-oblation,
and that is both the mandala-member and the mandala.
"In brief, the mind has the form of the assembly.

(HeTa I.x.43) "In brief" means from the perspective of the single aspect of all phenomena, namely, the aspect of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). "Mind" refers to the *bodhicitta*. "Having the form of the assembly" means that the gnosis (*jñāna*) which takes the form of the consecrations of the *dharmamudrā* and *mahāmudrā* is designated as the "True Assembly" (*satsamāja*).
The fourth chapter, the Exposition on the Result of Human Effort through the Samaya-mudrā, is completed.
Some manuscripts add: "This is the work of the venerable Nāgārjuna," which is indeed quite plausible, as evidenced by the following statement in the *Rāmapāla*:
"The *Sekoddeśa* [is] accompanied by the lineage of the *Caturmudrānvaya* composed by the venerable master Nāgārjuna."
Farewell.
